licensed.name: Anxiety
licensed.text: The eyebrows stay knitted, the eyes flick rapidly from side to side, the lower lip pulls between the teeth, and breathing remains shallow and quick. The hands grip together as the weight keeps shifting.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the thumb rubs the side of the finger, a lip bite, the eyes flick to the phone
- **Medium:** the brows stay knotted, the eyes dart left and right, the lower lip is caught between the teeth, the breath is quick and shallow, the hands grip each other while the weight shifts foot to foot
- **Explosive:** pacing in a small circle, both hands in the hair, the breath audible, the eyes darting to the door and back

licensed.name: Arc right
licensed.text: arc right. Movement: move on a shallow curved path around the main subject toward the right side. Speed: smooth measured curve. Framing: keep distance, height and subject readability consistent while the angle changes. End: finish from a new right-side angle.

licensed.name: Arc left

items.name: Coloured keyword in the caption
items.effect: The viewer learns the one word that matters in each line, even with the sound off.
items.use_when: Explainers that teach terms; any caption style that needs emphasis.
items.phrase: captions of about three words in white, the term being defined in the brand accent colour at the moment it is said

pitfalls.text: Colour only the word being defined. In the measured product explainer a colour on any other word is a listed failure.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

pitfalls.text: Four of the nine measured references highlight one word per caption by colour.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurements of published shorts (measured 22 and 23 Oct 2026)

source.note: Own words from our measurements of published shorts and Director Chair notes on Product UI as the explainer (Patchd)

items.name: Caption safe zones
items.effect: Text stays readable because the platform's buttons do not sit on it.
items.use_when: Every vertical video with text on it.
items.phrase: keep all text out of the top 160, the bottom 480 and the right 120 pixels of a 1080 by 1920 frame

pitfalls.text: These are planning values from a 2026 research report, not figures published by the platforms, and the interfaces change. Check the preview in the app before posting.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on b-roll and the Director Chair hook framework (our 2026 synthesis of @marco.thecreative's TikTok series, OpusClip's hook formulas, a Brandefy article, Meta retention research and a Gemini research report)

pitfalls.text: Keep text off the area where the captions sit, and away from the frame edges; devices crop differently.
pitfalls.source: The Director Chair hook framework (our 2026 synthesis of @marco.thecreative's TikTok series, OpusClip's hook formulas, a Brandefy article, Meta retention research and a Gemini research report)

source.note: Planning values our video QA checks, from Director Chair field notes on b-roll

items.body:
## Planning values on a 1080 by 1920 frame

| Platform | Top | Bottom | Right |
|---|---|---|---|
| TikTok | 160 px | 480 px | 120 px |
| Instagram Reels | 250 px | 320 px | 120 px |
| YouTube Shorts | 380 px | 380 px | 120 px |

Not published by the platforms. Treat them as a starting point and look at the in-app preview.

items.name: Sentence captions, revealed word by word
items.effect: Reads like a subtitle in a film: calm, and paced by the voice.
items.use_when: Narrated stories and brand films.
items.phrase: one sentence at a time, small white sans with no box, low centre, each word appearing as it is spoken

pitfalls.text: Measured on a 344-second story reel at 2.57 words per second, captions at about 76 percent of the frame height. Boxed, large or multi-sentence captions are the listed failures of this style.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, 23 Oct 2026

source.note: Own words from Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

items.name: Giant and knockout captions
items.effect: For one line the caption itself becomes the picture.
items.use_when: The loudest line of a talking-head video.
items.phrase: the caption box grows into a slab across the lower half of the frame, the words cut out of a cream block so the footage shows through the letters

pitfalls.text: The effect fires on the word that names it. In the measured list reel an effect more than 0.2 seconds off its word is a listed failure.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on Reel Kit (Justyn The AI Guy) (described from the frames of two clips; no result per effect was measured)

items.name: Cast block (identity lock)
items.effect: Each person keeps their face, build and clothes across every shot of a job.
items.use_when: Any video with recurring people.
items.phrase: one line per person with only what never changes: build, hair, face features, clothing, plus where they are from and how their voice sounds, repeated word for word in every prompt

pitfalls.text: Only invariants in the cast block; what changes per shot goes in the shot.
pitfalls.source: Rourke Heath (8 Aug 2026) via Director Chair field notes on video prompting

pitfalls.text: A fixed character in video needs the start frame and the character sheet in every job; the start frame shows only one angle.
pitfalls.source: House rule

items.effect: Formal, iconic, slightly uncanny; everything balances around the middle.
items.use_when: Architecture, product hero shots, stylised brand films.
items.phrase: perfectly centred, the corridor symmetrical on both sides, the person in the exact middle

items.effect: The viewer sees the structure of the video and where they are in it.
items.use_when: Breakdowns, launch films, how-it-was-made posts.
items.phrase: a labelled chapter bar with a moving playhead under the video frame, one label per beat

items.name: Face sheet
items.effect: Holds the face, hair and expression range of a character across shots.
items.use_when: Talking characters, close-ups, a persona that speaks to camera.
items.phrase: a row of face views of the same person: front, three-quarter both sides, profile, a natural smile and a neutral look, same light, plain background

pitfalls.text: More solo photographs make the real person: three gave a plausible stranger, eight gave the person. Never a group photo.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

pitfalls.text: The layout template leaks its own person; put it last with a take-nothing-else-from-it line.

items.name: Full-body character sheet
items.effect: One identity document that every later still and video binds, so the character stays the same.
items.use_when: Any recurring character, mascot or brand persona.
items.phrase: five equal columns at 21:9, one photograph per column: front, side, back, front close-up, top-down, a height ruler on the right, detail swatches and one data line

pitfalls.text: Run five columns at 21:9; at 16:9 the model stacks extra panels in the leftover width.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

pitfalls.text: Leave small details out of the sheet (a thin necklace, a small hat): they break at video resolution and shift the character.
pitfalls.source: Dan Kieft via Director Chair field notes on image prompting

pitfalls.text: Spell long labels letter by letter; never two-letter labels, they print the hyphens.

items.name: Chase shot
items.effect: Urgency: the camera struggles to keep up with fast action.
items.use_when: Action, sport, a playful chase in an ad.
items.phrase: chase shot, the camera runs behind him close and low, it lags, over-corrects and catches up again

pitfalls.text: For a camera that feels operated, describe how it fails: it lags behind, over-corrects, catches up.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting (rig wording from tested prompts)

licensed.name: Chase shot
licensed.text: chase shot. Movement: follow a moving subject quickly along the action route. Speed: fast, reactive and physically close. Framing: keep the subject visible while allowing energetic reframing. End: stay connected to the subject in motion.

## Move card

- **Camera:** runs after a fast subject, close
- **Pace:** fast and reactive
- **Keep:** the subject in view while the frame reframes roughly
- **Ends:** still on the subject's heels

items.name: Checklist with a counter
items.effect: The viewer watches the promise being kept item by item and stays to the end of the list.
items.use_when: List videos: N tips, N tools, N effects.
items.phrase: a checklist panel fills the right third from the first frame: numbered items, the current one highlighted in white, a counter 01 of 18 on top

pitfalls.text: Measured on the reference: 18 items in 20.5 seconds, 6.83 visual changes per 10 seconds, 8.3 percent of plays saved, 12 times the median of the account's other clips. The checklist is on screen from frame 0 and ticks on every item.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, 22 Oct 2026

pitfalls.text: No more items than seconds allow; faster than one item per second is the listed failure.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

source.note: Own words from Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

items.name: Chest level
items.effect: Close to eye level but a hair lower, so the person reads as present and a little taller.
items.use_when: Interviews, talking heads, handheld documentary work.
items.phrase: camera at chest height, looking straight at him, the lens a hand below his eye line

pitfalls.text: Angles given in degrees are often ignored. Say where the lens sits against the body (at her knee, at her hip) instead.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

items.name: Glitch hit on a beat
items.effect: A two-frame jolt that marks the beat.
items.use_when: Music-led edits, a hard reveal.
items.phrase: a chromatic split of the colour channels for two to four frames on the downbeat

pitfalls.text: Tested on 26 Oct 2026: the default amount of 8 pixels is barely visible on a soft image. Spike the amount for 2 to 4 frames on the hit.

items.effect: Handmade stop-motion clay: warm, funny, tactile.
items.use_when: Family brands, humour, food, kids.
items.phrase: stop-motion clay figures, fingerprints in the clay, slightly uneven handmade movement

items.effect: Emotion and detail: the viewer reads small changes in the face.
items.use_when: The moment of a reaction, a product touching skin, a decision.
items.phrase: close-up of her face from the chin to just above the hairline, the eyes in the upper third

pitfalls.text: Asking for a smile returns a generated smile. Describe what the eyes, mouth and breath do instead.

pitfalls.text: Perfect skin reads as AI. Ask for unretouched skin with pores and fine lines.

items.effect: Shows the goal is nearer than the viewer assumed.
items.use_when: Aspirational products, learning, fitness.

items.name: Confession
items.effect: An admitted mistake lowers the guard; the viewer stays for what changed.
items.use_when: Founders and experts, mid-funnel content.
items.phrase: I told clients for three years that they needed a film crew. I was wrong, and this is what changed my mind

pitfalls.text: Name the wrong belief, who confesses and the resolution. Without the resolution it is clickbait.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas (Motion's hook guide and 2026 creative benchmark, vendor data)

items.name: Conflict
items.effect: An accusation as the first line makes the viewer wait for the answer.
items.use_when: Local businesses, comedy, a twist that leads to the brand.
items.phrase: do not book a roofer before you have asked him this one question

pitfalls.text: Real, or staged and played for comedy. The brand enters as the twist after the tension resolves, never as the target of the accusation in earnest.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas

pitfalls.text: No fake news, fake emergencies or staged danger in real traffic. Show the trade's real risk safely, or generate the image and label it as AI.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas and Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

items.name: Confusion
items.effect: Something does not make sense; the viewer shares the question.
items.use_when: Before an explainer answers it, a problem statement, comedy.
items.phrase: one brow up and one down, the eyes search from point to point, the head tilts hard to one side, the mouth hangs a little open, the puzzled look grows instead of clearing

pitfalls.text: Never ask for a smile or for an emotion by name; describe the muscles. Asked-for smiles come back generated and forced.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting (client feedback, Aug 2026)

pitfalls.text: Put the trigger first (the door slams, she reads the message), then the performance. Without a trigger the reaction has no timing.
pitfalls.source: Dan Kieft and Higgsfield's tested prompts via Director Chair field notes on video prompting

licensed.name: Confusion
licensed.text: The eyebrows become asymmetric, one raised and one lowered. The eyes search rapidly, the head tilts sharply, and the mouth hangs slightly open. The puzzled expression deepens instead of resolving.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the brows draw together slightly, the head tilts a few degrees, the eyes narrow
- **Medium:** one brow up and one down, the eyes search from point to point, the head tilts hard to one side, the mouth hangs a little open, the puzzled look grows instead of clearing
- **Explosive:** both hands open at the sides, the head pushes forward, the face scrunches, a look around the room for someone to explain

items.name: Old way, new way
items.effect: Two states side by side let the viewer place themselves in the worse one.
items.use_when: Tools and methods that replace a habit.
items.phrase: the old way: three days in an edit suite. The new way: one take and a reference reel

pitfalls.text: Position against the old way or the whole category, not a named competitor; a split screen is the standard execution.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas (Motion's hook guide and 2026 creative benchmark, vendor data)

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas

items.name: Contrast in four levels
items.effect: Tells you before you generate whether an idea is strange enough to stop a scroll.
items.use_when: Scoring a concept for a still or an opening shot.
items.phrase: level 1, the delivery robot slumped at a bus stop; level 2, the same robot in a fur coat; level 3, holding a wilted flower and looking down the empty road

pitfalls.text: The four levels: in the place it belongs, in an unexpected situation, plus unexpected styling, plus feeling. The creator's claim is that social images stop the scroll from level 1 up; not measured by us.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 realism (Dan Kieft)

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 realism (Dan Kieft)

items.name: Presenter in the corner
items.effect: The content gets the whole frame and still has a face attached.
items.use_when: Motion-graphics explainers with a host.
items.phrase: the presenter as a cut-out in the bottom-left corner, about 30 percent of the width and the lowest quarter of the height, the caption chip to their right

pitfalls.text: The presenter stays in one corner for the full length and never covers the card being read.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

source.note: Own words from Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

items.name: Count-up number
items.effect: A number that climbs feels earned, and the viewer waits to see where it stops.
items.use_when: Stats, results, a hook built on one figure.
items.phrase: the number counts up from 0 to 87 inside a ring that fills, a soft tick on each step

pitfalls.text: A counter that sets its text on load shows the final number on frame 0. Review frame 0 and the frames either side of every cut.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Video from code at Anfloy (Dima Bilous)

pitfalls.text: An exact figure reads as real and a rounded one as made up: 87, not about 100.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on motion graphics and Director Chair notes on Video from code at Anfloy (Dima Bilous)

items.name: Cowboy shot
items.effect: A confident, ready-to-act stance; the frame stops just below the hands at the hips.
items.use_when: Hero shots of a founder, a team lead or a character about to act.
items.phrase: cowboy shot, framed from mid-thigh up, hands visible at hip height, the camera slightly below eye level

pitfalls.text: Name the cut line on the body (mid-thigh). A model that only hears the term often returns a medium shot.
pitfalls.source: Not measured yet, check on the first example

per_model.phrase: Compose a cinematic cowboy shot, framing the subject from the mid-thighs up to emphasize their stance and immediate surroundings.

items.name: Crash zoom
items.effect: A jolt: sudden emphasis, often comic or dramatic.
items.use_when: Reaction shots, mockumentary humour, a reveal that should feel like a punchline.
items.phrase: crash zoom onto his face, a snap from medium shot to tight close-up in a fraction of a second

pitfalls.text: Crash zooms add chaotic energy; use one per sequence or they cancel each other out.

items.name: Creator ads paid on performance
items.effect: Many different ads from people who use the product, paid for by what performs.
items.use_when: Self-serve products with organic pull and a Meta budget.
items.phrase: pay each creator a share of the spend behind their own ads, with a monthly floor for a video quota, and give them the product and the news, not a script

pitfalls.text: One company's account of its own programme: 50 creators making 500 to 600 ads a month. The money figures are the builder's own and the spend behind them is not given.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Paid UGC on performance (Hector Serrano, Wispr Flow)

pitfalls.text: Keep ads different in person, setting, words or format. Meta's own engineering post says similar ads get overlapping codes; the often-quoted 60 percent cut-off has no Meta source.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Paid UGC on performance (Hector Serrano, Wispr Flow)

pitfalls.text: Choose creators for the gaps in the ad library, one per kind of buyer, not for follower numbers.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Paid UGC on performance (Hector Serrano, Wispr Flow)

items.use_when: Emotional storytelling, reunions, charity.

pitfalls.text: Never ask for a smile or for an emotion by name; describe the muscles. Asked-for smiles come back generated and forced.

pitfalls.text: Put the trigger first (the door slams, she reads the message), then the performance. Without a trigger the reaction has no timing.

licensed.name: Crying
licensed.text: The eyes and nose flush red, tears spill over the lower lid, the breath catches in visible stutters, the mouth pulls into a square shape, and the chin crumples and trembles. The shoulders begin to shake.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the eyes glaze and redden, the lips press together, one hard swallow
- **Medium:** the eyes and nose redden, tears run over the lower lids, the breath stutters, the mouth pulls square, the chin crumples and shakes, the shoulders start to move
- **Explosive:** the face folds completely, loud uneven sobs, the body curls forward, hands over the eyes, the shoulders heave

items.name: Everything is in the caption
items.effect: Giving the whole method away earns saves and trust.
items.use_when: Tutorials and tool lists, when saves matter more than a list of contacts.
items.phrase: no message needed, the full list is in the caption, said while pointing down

pitfalls.text: Measured on one tutorial: 11 percent of plays saved at 72 times the account's median, against 2.6 percent saved for a comment-keyword clip read the same week, which got seven times the comments.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on One prompt edit (Payton Kaleiwahea, Mino)

pitfalls.text: Pick by the goal: saves and trust, or comments and a list.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas

items.name: Comment keyword
items.effect: One word in the comments starts a private conversation and feeds reach.
items.use_when: Organic posts that build a list.
items.phrase: comment the word EDIT and I will send you the link, while a comment box on screen types the word

pitfalls.text: It trades saves for comments. Read in the same week: a keyword clip got 1.4 percent comments and 2.6 percent saves; a clip that gave everything in its caption got 0.2 percent comments and 11 percent saves.

pitfalls.text: A keyword needs something real behind it. In the measured clip the automated message only reached people who followed the account, which adds a step.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026 and Director Chair notes on One prompt edit (Payton Kaleiwahea, Mino)

items.phrase: start with the result and hold back how: this cost us 40 euro and replaced a whole shoot, here is the trick

items.effect: One thing out of place makes the viewer wait for the explanation.
items.use_when: Products and services with no natural drama.
items.phrase: a three-seat sofa stands in the middle of a supermarket aisle and shoppers steer their trolleys around it

pitfalls.text: The honest brand version is the product in a place it does not belong, explained by the payoff.

pitfalls.text: An interrupt with no link to the message loses viewers at 5 to 10 seconds.

items.name: Cut on action
items.effect: Cuts that land during a movement feel fast and invisible.
items.use_when: Face cam edits, B-roll sequences, the step from hook to content.
items.phrase: cut in the middle of the hand movement and continue it from a different angle in the next shot

pitfalls.text: Hard cuts land on movement or a beat, never on a still pose.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

pitfalls.text: Cut at the peak of the motion, not before or after it, and film the same action from at least two angles.

items.name: Cut on the end of a sentence
items.effect: The picture changes when the thought does, so a slow film still feels edited.
items.use_when: Voice-over stories and brand films with long holds.
items.phrase: hold each scene on a slow push and cut on the last word of the sentence

pitfalls.text: A story reel measured at 2.03 changes per 10 seconds with a median hold of 4.1 seconds cuts this way; a scene change in mid-sentence is its listed failure.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, 23 Oct 2026

items.name: Cut on the beat
items.effect: The edit feels locked to the music.
items.use_when: Music-led montages, launch films, showreels.
items.phrase: every cut and reveal lands on a beat of the music, and the big hits land on the first beat of a bar

pitfalls.text: Build to a grid from the tempo: at 120 beats per minute and 30 frames per second a beat is 15 frames, so a four-beat scene is 60 frames.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on motion graphics

pitfalls.text: Lock the picture before the sound goes on. Any change after that breaks the timing.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Let one element react to the audio level. The whole frame reacting reads as a screensaver.

items.name: Cut to a new camera on the line
items.effect: One take feels like a multi-camera shoot.
items.use_when: Interviews and talking heads filmed on one camera.
items.phrase: at 2.6 seconds, on the line that names the second camera, cut to a position 45 degrees to her right at eye height, the bookshelf now behind her

pitfalls.text: Let the dialogue direct the cuts: cut on a line or a clear action about every 3 to 4 seconds, and make back-to-back shots different sizes.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: In the creator's own demo it took three or four generations per sequence and one kept clip has a gesture that lands late. Keep the filmed take as the master and interleave the new angles.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Describe left and right by landmarks in the room; bare left and right flip.

items.name: Deep focus
items.effect: Everything sharp from front to back; the viewer can look anywhere.
items.use_when: Landscapes, architecture, a busy scene where context matters.
items.phrase: deep focus, the flowers in the foreground and the mountains behind equally sharp

pitfalls.text: For stills, practitioners write a full capture line with an aperture (35mm, f/1.8); a 2025 study for Midjourney found f-stops ignored and plain words (blurred background) working. Plain words first, the number as support.

items.name: Definition card

items.use_when: Product explainers and teaching series.

items.name: The result in the hook
items.effect: The promise is delivered before it is explained.
items.use_when: Anything with an audible or visible before and after.
items.phrase: she says this mic has nothing on it, and in the middle of the sentence the sound changes to the processed version; below her, six empty numbered slots wait

pitfalls.text: Measured on the reference file: across the hook line the noise floor drops 7.4 dB, and the empty six-slot list is already on frame 0. The clip reached about 50 times the median of the account's other recent clips.

items.effect: A coded scene looks shot on a camera.
items.use_when: Interface and product animations built from flat layers.

items.name: Determination
items.effect: Resolve settling in; the person is going to do it.
items.use_when: Sport, founders, the turn in a story, call to action.
items.phrase: the eyes lift and lock on a point ahead, a deep breath fills the chest, the jaw sets at the hinge, the eyes narrow, the shoulders roll back, one firm nod

pitfalls.text: Never ask for a smile or for an emotion by name; describe the muscles. Asked-for smiles come back generated and forced.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting (client feedback, Aug 2026)

pitfalls.text: Put the trigger first (the door slams, she reads the message), then the performance. Without a trigger the reaction has no timing.

licensed.name: Determination

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the jaw sets, the gaze fixes forward
- **Medium:** the eyes lift and lock on a point ahead, a deep breath fills the chest, the jaw sets at the hinge, the eyes narrow, the shoulders roll back, one firm nod
- **Explosive:** the fists close, a sharp exhale, the body rises from the chair, the first step forward is already taken

pitfalls.text: Put a real screenshot or a screen recording in the frame; a drawn stand-in is the fallback, never the plan.

pitfalls.text: Grain, sensor noise and vignetting date an image: a shop scene with them read as a photo from 2008. Grain belongs to a film or snapshot register, not to realism as such.

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the nose wrinkles slightly, the upper lip lifts on one side
- **Medium:** the nose wrinkles hard and drags the upper lip up, the eyes squint almost shut, the chin pulls in, the head turns away and back, the look of revulsion stays

pitfalls.text: Write the move as behaviour with a start and an end (a slow straight push from six metres to three and a half). A bare move name drifts.

source.note: Our own reading and measurement of a TikTok by @pro.glitch, posted 18 Oct 2026. The clip is a third-party reference and is not shown; the words here are ours

items.body:
## Measured on the reference

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| Length | 223.1 s |
| Aspect | 9:16 |
| Visual changes per 10 s | 1.03 |
| Median segment | 9.22 s |
| First visual change | 9.17 s |
| First spoken word | 0.0 s |
| Spoken words per second | 3.26 |
| Loudness, integrated | -14.2 LUFS |
| True peak | -1.4 dBTP |
| Sound floor | -79.8 dBFS (clean silences, no music) |
| Face in sampled frames | the presenter is a cartoon in every frame; the face detector counts 14 percent |
| Plays, saves | 40,900 plays, 6.5 percent saved (read 23 Oct 2026) |
| Against the account's median | 6.9 times |

## The recipe

1. Stack the frame: the presenter on top at about 39 percent of the height, one continuous locked shot; a whiteboard canvas below at about 61 percent, hand-drawn style on white.
2. Frame 0: the first board already drawn with the promise of the video in two or three shapes. The first word is on frame 0.
3. For each numbered point: clear to a fresh area, write the number in a coloured circle and the heading, then draw each shape and word at the moment it is said, led by a labelled cursor. Type text letter by letter.
4. A cleared section lands about once every 8 to 12 seconds, with small strokes all the time in between.
5. End on a row of all the numbered circles as a recap, then the call to action.
6. Captions of two words (one to three), white bold sans on a dark rounded box at the foot of the presenter zone, the spoken word in the accent colour.
7. No music, no sound effects. Voice at -14 LUFS, true peak at or under -1.5 dBTP.

## Not for

Emotional stories, testimonials, product beauty, luxury brands, anything under 45 seconds.

## The recipe

2. Place the presenter as a cut-out in the bottom-left corner, about 30 percent of the width and the lowest quarter of the height, for the whole video.

Emotional stories, testimonials, product beauty, live-action brands, anything under 30 seconds.

## The recipe

## The recipe

1. Write the script as one person's story in dated chapters, each turn anchored on a real source. Narrate in the first person at about 2.5 words per second.
2. Build each chapter as a low-poly 3D set with soft light and shallow depth of field. Cast anonymous figures and one narrator figure.
3. Hold each set with a slow push or drift and cut at the end of a sentence: 1.5 to 2.5 changes per 10 seconds, holds of 3 to 5 seconds.
4. Whenever a fact is stated, cut to a figure holding the printed source page to camera, readable.
5. Captions: one sentence at a time, small white sans with no box, revealed word by word, low centre.
6. A quiet ambient bed under the voice; sound effects only where the story has an object. Voice at -14 LUFS.

## Not for

Step lists, tool tutorials, lead magnets, product demos, anything under 60 seconds.

items.name: Four starter edit styles
items.effect: A take gets a look that fits what kind of take it is.
items.use_when: Editing a filmed talking head when there is no reference reel yet.

pitfalls.text: What an automatic edit copies from a reference: caption words, case and box, the layout and how tight the pauses are. Not copied: moving captions, zooms inside a shot, colour, music and B-roll.

items.body:
## The four starters

| Starter | What it looks like | Pace of the clip it was measured from | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Centre captions | the take fills the frame, a light punch-in on every other segment, two-word captions in the middle on a black box | 2.6 changes per 10 s | an opinion, a founder update, a story |
| Screen teacher | the take or the product screen full frame, three-word captions low, one keyword in the accent colour | 2.0 changes per 10 s | a tutorial or a product walkthrough |
| Speaker over a board | the speaker in the top third, a board below for a list, a screenshot or a product | 4.7 changes per 10 s | an explainer with at least three things to show |
| Fast list | a punch-in on every other segment, two-word outlined captions low | 6.8 changes per 10 s | tips, a list, a recap |

licensed.name: Embarrassment
licensed.text: Color rises in the cheeks, the eyes dart down and to the side, and an awkward pressed-lip half-smile appears. The head ducks and turns away while one hand rises near the mouth. The eyes stay lowered.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the cheeks colour, the eyes drop for a moment
- **Medium:** her face goes pink, she looks at the floor beside her, presses her lips into a tight awkward half-smile, ducks her head to the side and lifts a hand toward her mouth, and does not look up again
- **Explosive:** the face hidden in both hands, the body turning away, a pained laugh, the ears red

licensed.name: Exhaustion
licensed.text: The eyelids drag downward, a long blink stays closed too long, the head drifts down and lifts again slowly, the jaw hangs slack, and one long breath empties out. The eyes reopen only halfway.

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** a heavy blink, the shoulders sag
- **Medium:** his eyes close for a second too long, his head nods forward and he pulls it back up, his mouth hangs a little open, he lets out one long empty breath, and his eyes open only halfway
- **Explosive:** the body slides down the wall to sit on the floor, the head back against it, the eyes closed, the arms limp

## Three intensities

licensed.name: Fast zoom in
licensed.text: fast zoom in. Movement: quickly increase lens focal length toward the main visual target. Speed: quick decisive zoom. Framing: keep the target centered or clearly readable during the scale change. End: finish on a stable tighter composition.

items.body:
## Values the Camera Control stage uses

The stage reads the framing off the 3D scene and writes it into its prompt. Its values, in our words:

- **Size**, from how much of the frame the person fills: extreme close-up, close-up, medium close-up, medium, medium-wide, wide, extreme wide. Tighter sizes are paired with more skin detail and shallower focus, wider ones with deep focus.
- **Side**: front, front three-quarter (left or right), profile (left or right), rear three-quarter (left or right), back.
- **Height**: ground level, knee level, hip level, chest level, eye level, high angle, overhead.
- **Lens**: a vertical field of view from 14 to 90 degrees, written as the nearest of 14, 18, 24, 28, 35, 50, 85, 100 or 135mm.
- **Presets**: medium, wide, close-up, low angle, high angle, over the shoulder, two shot.
- **Moves** (video): static, push in, pull out, pan, tilt, tracking, orbit, crane, handheld, crash zoom, dolly zoom, whip pan, aerial, or your own.
- **Staging**: one or two people, each placed left or right, nearer or further, and turned; a pose per person; a rule-of-thirds overlay; a shot view and a plan view from above.
- **Sheets**: a character sheet or an environment sheet can stand in for the written subject and place.

## Translations to start from

- **Thriller:** low-key side light, cold grade, longer lenses, tight frames
- **Horror:** underlight or darkness, wide lens close to the face, long holds
- **Western:** hard sun, wide exteriors, low angles, warm brown grade

items.body:
## The prompt, in order

1. **What the image is for:** a product photograph, an advertisement, a diagram.
2. **The visible details:** materials, light, colours, medium, scale.
3. **People:** framing of the body, relative size, where they look, what they do with objects.
4. **Text:** the exact words in quotes, with position and type; unusual words and brand names spelled letter by letter.
5. **Exclusions,** short and grouped: no extra text, no watermark, no logo.

## Edits
Change one thing per round and repeat the list of what must stay (identity, layout, light, labels) every round; details drift across repeated edits.

## What we measured (Sep 2026)
A city name drew the wrong city's architecture; name the materials instead (brick with blue stone).

items.body:
## The prompt, in order

1. **Subject** with the same descriptor every time it is mentioned.
2. **Visible action:** what the body does, not what the person feels.
3. **Scene.**
4. **Camera language:** one main move.
5. **Light and mood.**

## Multi-shot
Give each shot its duration, framing, angle, action and move. Label every speaker and write the action before the line.

## Weak spots
Counts are unreliable, complex physics is hard, and character drift is the biggest problem; repeat the same descriptor.

items.body:
## The steps

1. **Find the frame.** Search a film-still library (ShotDeck, paid; Flim, a free tier with one download a day) or scroll it like a feed and keep the frames that stop you.
2. **Read its data.** ShotDeck shows a data panel per still: colour, aspect ratio, format, lighting, time of day, camera, lenses, film stock. Note those values; on Flim, describe them yourself.
3. **Write the look block:** the capture (camera, lenses, stock, ratio), the light (type, time of day), the grade as words with their place in the frame, the hex codes beside them for the edit.
4. **Paste it word for word** into every prompt of the job.
5. **Optionally attach the still** as a look reference: take its light, lens character and grade, none of its people or its place.

A film still is someone else's copyright: a reference for the look, never material in the output, and never published.

items.body:
## The prompt, in order

1. **Reference roles,** one line each, including what not to take from each image (keep the face, do not take the background).
2. **One paragraph of full sentences,** never a comma list: the register first (candid, editorial, documentary), then the subject in a physical state doing one thing, the real place, where the camera stands, the light and where it comes from.
3. **A capture line:** lens, aperture or depth, grain or none, the grade, the direction of the light.
4. **Text** in quotes with its position. Otherwise signs, screens and packaging carry no letters.

## What we measured (June to Sep 2026)

- Early words weigh most: the register goes in the first sentence.
- Positive descriptions beat bans; an exclusion works for what not to take from a reference and for an attribute of a named object.
- The same prompt in another ratio drifts; give the approved image back as a reference.

items.name: Prompt guide: Seedance 2.5
items.effect: Scenes of up to 30 seconds that hold their characters, look and timing.
items.use_when: Multi-shot scenes, dialogue, ads with a story, edits on real footage.
items.phrase: one continuous block in labelled sections: the look first, the scene, the cast, the place, the first frame and who stands where, then each shot on its own timecode, then optics, camera, physics, light, and the sound last

pitfalls.text: Skip a section and the output fails in a predictable way; the tested prompts include all of them.
pitfalls.source: Higgsfield Seedance 2.5 prompting guide, read 28 Sep 2026

pitfalls.text: When the lines come back scrambled or the speech speeds up, the prompt asks for more than the duration holds; split the scene.

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on video prompting and the Higgsfield guide summary

items.body:
## The prompt, in order

1. **Global look:** camera, lens, stock, light, grade, one block, the same words in every prompt of the job.
2. **Scene:** what happens, in two sentences.
3. **Cast:** one line per person with only what never changes, plus their voice.
4. **Place:** the location, its light, what is in it.
5. **First frame and blocking:** who stands where, as positions in the frame.
6. **Shots:** each with its own timecode, framing, action and the kind of cut into the next.
7. **Optics and camera:** field of view in degrees plus distance; one main move per shot.
8. **Physics and light:** what changes one way only, what repeats as a rule, where the light comes from.
9. **Sound:** ambience, effects, music, the spoken lines with their delivery.

Every rule that must never break gets its own named lock (how many people exist, who stays on which side).

## Lengths
One generation holds about 30 seconds. A longer script is split at a hand-off into parts that cut together, each carrying the same look and cast blocks.

items.body:
## The parts, kept apart

1. **First frame or blocking.** Attach your start image, or block the frame first in a 3D stage (Camera Control) and export it as the composition reference.
2. **Subject** and **place**: only what the image does not already show.
3. **Camera move:** one move, written as a move card (camera, pace, keep, ends).
4. **Action:** what the person does, as behaviour with a trigger.
5. **Look:** the job's look sentence, the same in every prompt.
6. **Sheets:** say whether a character sheet or an environment sheet is attached, and give each its role.

Both free tools we point to work this way: the move library keeps the camera line apart from the scene, and the 3D stage asks for subject, environment, camera move and look as separate fields.

items.body:
## The prompt, in order

1. **Camera first,** one move or a hold. The first thing named gets the most attention.
2. **The action as behaviour, in order,** with its pace and where it ends.
3. **The sound** in its own sentence: the ambience, the one effect that matters, the spoken line and how it is said.
4. **What stays:** framing and subject as in the start image.
5. **The look** as one sentence, the same in every clip of the job.

## Notes
The start frame carries the look and the detail; keep the Veo prompt simple. For dialogue, keep speech under 8 seconds and ask for no subtitles.

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the eyes slide away from the other person, the lips tighten, a small swallow
- **Medium:** the mouth opens to speak and closes again, the gaze drops to the floor and stays there, the head lowers, the throat moves on a hard swallow, a hand rubs the back of the neck
- **Explosive:** the face turns fully away, both hands cover the mouth, the eyes squeeze shut, the shoulders curl in

items.name: Laughter
items.effect: Real, uncontrolled amusement the viewer wants to share.
items.use_when: Comedy beats, friends, a product moment that delights.
items.phrase: the laugh starts in the chest, the shoulders shake, the eyes narrow into creases, the head tips back once and comes forward, a grin stays after the sound stops

pitfalls.text: Never ask for a smile or for an emotion by name; describe the muscles. Asked-for smiles come back generated and forced.

pitfalls.text: Put the trigger first (the door slams, she reads the message), then the performance. Without a trigger the reaction has no timing.

licensed.name: Joy / Laughter
licensed.text: The eyes squeeze into crinkled slits, the mouth opens wide showing teeth, the head drops forward and tips back, and the shoulders bounce with each breath. The laugh settles into a wide lingering grin.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** a breath escapes through the nose, the cheeks rise and the lips press shut to hold it in, the eyes stay amused
- **Medium:** the laugh starts in the chest, the shoulders shake, the eyes narrow into creases, the head tips back once and comes forward, a grin stays after the sound stops
- **Explosive:** the whole upper body folds forward, one hand slaps the table, eyes squeezed shut and wet at the corners, the laugh runs out of breath and restarts once

items.name: Loudness target
items.effect: The video sits at the level of its neighbours in the feed and does not distort.
items.use_when: Every export.

pitfalls.text: Measured across nine reference edits: integrated loudness runs from -18.7 to -8.2 LUFS, and six of them sit between -15.2 and -14.1.

pitfalls.text: -14 LUFS is a common convention for social video, not a figure the platforms publish for uploads. The true peak matters most.

items.body:
## Starting points

| Kind of video | Mood |

| Data reveal, myth busting | a subtle tension beat that builds |

items.name: Music bed under the voice
items.effect: Carries the mood without costing a word.
items.use_when: Stories, diaries and ads; often left out of teaching videos.
items.phrase: an instrumental bed under the voice, lowered whenever she speaks

pitfalls.text: Three of the nine measured reference edits have clean silences between the words, a sound floor under -48 dBFS, so no continuous bed. They are the three teaching boards.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurements of published shorts (nine entries, measured 22 and 23 Oct 2026)

pitfalls.text: The framework's rule of thumb is music at 10 to 15 percent of the voice. Our editor starts the bed at -18 dB and ducks it under the voice.

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the mouth smiles but the eyes stay flat, one quick swallow
- **Medium:** the mouth stretches wide while the eyes do not crease at all, the blinking speeds up, a hard swallow, the gaze drops and the strained smile snaps back on
- **Explosive:** a grin frozen too long, a laugh that comes out too high, the eyes darting for an exit, sweat on the temple

items.use_when: Ads, stock-like scenes, any group of people.

items.effect: Visible brushstrokes and rich colour: classic, artful.
items.use_when: Premium editorial, art-directed campaigns, portraits.
items.phrase: oil painting, thick visible brushstrokes, rich blended colour, canvas texture

items.name: One clock for picture and sound
items.effect: Every sound lands on its frame, and stays there when the edit is re-timed.
items.use_when: Code-rendered video with typing, counters or many cues.
items.phrase: one list of event times drives the animation, the key presses and the sound cues

pitfalls.text: In a 59-second 3D film one file holds the time of all 50 typed characters. The screen, the keys and the click track read it, which is why a key drops on the frame its letter appears.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on A Blender film from one request (Riley Brown, Claude Fable 5.2)

pitfalls.text: Name each sound cue by its event, not by a time, and print every cue's offset from its beat: more than one frame is a bug.

items.name: One promise, a few formats, one slot
items.effect: A stranger understands what the account is for from any single post.
items.use_when: Running an account as a series.
items.phrase: write the account's promise in one line; every post keeps it, in two or three repeatable formats, at one fixed time in the audience's evening

pitfalls.text: On one measured account the median of the ten posts after a change of promise was 33.6 times the ten before; the formats had not changed. One account cannot prove the cause; it is the only visible change.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

pitfalls.text: A step wears off: the median fell to about a quarter between the first and the second half of October, as the examples began to repeat. Change the sources before changing the format.

items.effect: Continuity across cuts: wet stays wet, a bitten apple never grows back.
items.use_when: Any change that builds over a scene.

items.name: Openings that lose the viewer
items.effect: Knowing what wastes the first second is half of writing a hook.
items.use_when: Checking a first cut before it is posted.
items.phrase: no greeting, no logo and no context: the first frame is the moment itself, with the first word on it

pitfalls.text: A slow fade-in, a title card, a greeting, the brand name first, context before tension, a question nobody asked: each spends the first second on nothing.

## Move card

- **Camera:** circles the subject at a fixed distance
- **Pace:** smooth
- **Keep:** the subject in the centre while the background turns
- **Ends:** a full or planned part circle

items.name: Pace in visual changes per 10 seconds
items.effect: The viewer always has something new to look at, at a rate the content can carry.
items.use_when: Planning an edit and checking a render against a reference.

pitfalls.text: Visual changes are not cuts: a punch-in, a big graphic change or a board move counts. In a split layout the speaker can stay one take.

licensed.name: Pain / Wince
licensed.text: The eyes clamp shut, the teeth bare in a hard grimace, the head snaps to one side, and one shoulder rises toward the ear. The face stays contracted before easing only slightly.

source.note: Families, intensities and emotion names from Emotion Direction (names and structure only, read 13 Oct 2026); the directions are our own words in its grammar: body parts in the order they move, ending on what holds. Rules from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** a quick flinch, the eyes shut for a moment, a breath in through the teeth
- **Medium:** he sucks air in through clenched teeth, screws his eyes shut, jerks his head away from the pain and hunches that shoulder up, and his face stays tight for a long moment before it softens a little
- **Explosive:** doubling over, a hand grabbing the injured spot, a cry cut short, rocking on the spot

items.name: Pan (left or right)
items.effect: Scans a space or follows something across it, like turning your head.
items.use_when: Revealing a room, following a person who walks past, showing a row of products.
items.phrase: slow pan to the right, the camera turns on its tripod and stays in one place, new space comes in from the right edge

pitfalls.text: Give one main camera move per shot. Two moves at once, or orders that contradict each other, make the camera wander.
pitfalls.source: Kling camera guide and ByteDance Dreamina Seedance guide, via Director Chair field notes on video prompting

pitfalls.text: A slow pan gives a landscape time to render detail; a fast one smears it.

items.name: Pass through
items.effect: Goes through a surface into a new space; a playful reveal.
items.use_when: Through a window into a room, through a product into its inside.
items.phrase: the camera glides toward the shop window and passes through the glass into the room behind it

pitfalls.text: Give one main camera move per shot. Two moves at once, or orders that contradict each other, make the camera wander.

licensed.name: Pass-through objects
licensed.text: pass-through movement. Movement: move forward toward a visible object, surface or barrier and continue into the space beyond. Speed: smooth centered glide. Framing: keep the opening or surface centered as the transition point. End: arrive inside the revealed space beyond.

## Move card

- **Camera:** travels toward a surface and through it
- **Pace:** smooth
- **Keep:** the opening or surface centred until it passes
- **Ends:** inside the space beyond

items.name: Pattern interrupt
items.effect: Breaks the scroll with something the viewer did not expect.
items.use_when: Crowded feeds, low-interest categories.
items.phrase: open on an action nobody expects in this setting: the founder drops the product into a bucket of water and keeps talking

pitfalls.text: Hooks are judged by the first two seconds of retention on the platform. Test two openings of the same video instead of trusting a formula.

items.name: Pedestal (up or down)
items.effect: Lifts or lowers the viewer's eye line without tilting; a calm vertical reveal.
items.use_when: Rising from a table top to the person behind it, or lowering to a product.
items.phrase: pedestal up, the whole camera rises straight up from table height to her face, the lens stays level

pitfalls.text: A tilt turns the camera; a pedestal moves it up or down and keeps the lens level. Name the one you want.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

external_refs.what: a looping example clip of this move and a free prompt card (link only)

licensed.name: Pedestal up
licensed.text: pedestal up. Movement: move the entire camera vertically upward in a straight line. Speed: smooth constant lift. Framing: keep the lens level and pointed in the same direction during the vertical move. End: finish with the higher framing clearly readable.

licensed.name: Pedestal down
licensed.text: pedestal down. Movement: move the entire camera vertically downward in a straight line. Speed: smooth constant descent. Framing: keep the lens level and pointed in the same direction during the vertical move. End: finish with the lower framing clearly readable.

source.note: Move names and the seven groups from aicameramovements.com (names and structure only); behaviour and numbers in our own words from Director Chair field notes on video prompting and the first Director Chair spec

items.body:

items.effect: Reads as a real person filming themselves: direct, unpolished, believable.
items.use_when: Creator content, testimonials, social ads that must not look like ads.

items.effect: Proof that looks like something the viewer has seen on their own phone.
items.use_when: Results, social proof, a comment or message call to action.
items.phrase: a card of the earlier post floats in the top fifth of the frame, its comment counter climbing as he says the number

pitfalls.text: Every number on a card is a real one, readable at phone size, and the receipt lands on the word that claims it.

items.name: Polaroid instant
items.effect: Flash, faded colours and a white frame: a personal, vintage snapshot.
items.use_when: Party content, nostalgia, personal moments.
items.phrase: Polaroid instant photo, direct flash, soft focus, faded colours

pitfalls.text: Grain, sensor noise and vignetting date an image: a shop scene with them read as a photo from 2008. Grain belongs to a film or snapshot register, not to realism as such.

items.name: Portrait (85mm)
items.effect: Flatters faces and softens the background; the person is the subject.
items.use_when: Close-ups, interviews, dialogue singles, headshots.
items.phrase: 85mm portrait lens, the face in close-up, the background soft and compressed behind her

pitfalls.text: For stills, practitioners write a full capture line with an aperture (35mm, f/1.8); a 2025 study for Midjourney found f-stops ignored and plain words (blurred background) working. Plain words first, the number as support.
pitfalls.source: Dan Kieft (1 Sep 2026) via Director Chair field notes on image prompting; Midjourney mapping in our own notes (2025, to audit)

pitfalls.text: Degrees mean different things per tool: Camera Control uses a vertical field of view (29 degrees is about 50mm), Higgsfield's tested prompts a diagonal one (29 degrees is about 85mm). Say which, or give the focal length.
pitfalls.source: Camera Control (aicameracontrol.com), its framing label read on 13 Oct 2026 by placing the subject in the 3D stage and Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.phrase: she kneels on one knee, her weight on the back foot, both hands resting on the raised knee

pitfalls.text: Write the pose as the parts of the body and where the weight sits, not as a mood word.

items.body:
## Stances to start from

- **Alert:** standing, weight forward, head up, ready to move
- **Crouched:** low to the ground, one hand on the floor
- **Kneeling:** down on one knee
- **Fallen:** lying where they dropped
- **Asleep:** lying down, the body loose
- **Braced:** fists up, feet apart
- **Slumped:** head lowered, shoulders dropped

items.name: POV phone scroll
items.effect: The viewer sees exactly what using it looks like.
items.use_when: Apps, shops, booking flows, anything done on a phone.
items.phrase: over-the-shoulder on a hand holding the phone, the thumb scrolling the results and tapping one

pitfalls.text: Use a real screen recording for the interface. Product screens come from recordings in the edit, never from the video model.

items.effect: The viewer becomes the person and sees through their eyes.
items.use_when: Creator-style demos, first-person product use, what my day looks like.
items.phrase: point-of-view shot, the camera is her eyes, her own hands visible at the bottom of the frame holding the product

pitfalls.text: Give the viewpoint a reason: this is taken from her own chair, the camera is her eyes, she is not in the picture. A motivated viewpoint holds where a ban is ignored.

items.effect: Frames the clip as a moment, in the feed's own handwriting.
items.use_when: Selfie diaries, relatable openers.
items.phrase: a two-line title that starts with POV in the platform's own text style, white with a black stroke, in the top fifth for the first half of the video

items.use_when: Homes, cafés, bars, evening interiors.
items.phrase: lit by the lamps in the room: a desk lamp beside him and a pendant over the table, warm pools of light

items.name: More angles from one take
items.effect: One filmed take gains close-ups, low angles and profiles without a second camera.
items.use_when: Founder videos and interviews shot on one phone.
items.phrase: hold the person, the words, the lip sync, the room and the light exactly as filmed and change nothing but the camera; then one line per shot with its timecode and where the camera stands

pitfalls.text: Budget three or four generations per sequence and cut the good seconds from each; in the creator's own example the first two attempts kept the wrong angle.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Keep the prompt short, 120 to 200 words. His stated reason: long prompts drift back to the original angle.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Priced by our CLI on 22 Oct 2026 at 16 credits a second at 1080p: a 22-second sequence is about 350 credits per attempt.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Our own measurement in video edit mode found one camera change per run; the reference mode he uses is not yet run by us.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

per_model.phrase: the clip in the video reference slot, a duration one second longer than the clip, one scope line that locks everything but the camera, then one timecoded line per shot that says where the camera physically is

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 infinite angles (Rourke Heath)

items.name: B-roll pass: show or explain
items.effect: Every line that needs a picture gets one, and the brand's library grows with each video.
items.use_when: Any edit of a talking take or a script before a shoot.
items.phrase: for each line ask whether a picture must show something concrete or explain something abstract; film the concrete, animate the abstract, and pitch at most three new ideas per video

pitfalls.text: Ideas only until approved: two or three directions as stills first, and only the chosen one is animated.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on B-roll that pitches itself (Josh Blatchford) and Director Chair field notes on b-roll

pitfalls.text: Search the brand's own footage and existing graphics before pitching anything new. Generation comes last, with the credits shown first.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on B-roll that pitches itself (Josh Blatchford)

pitfalls.text: Build a graphic as a template with its values as inputs, so the next video reuses it with new data.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on b-roll

pitfalls.text: A graphic stays on screen long enough to read: at least 1.5 seconds plus about 0.3 seconds per word on it. A house rule of thumb, not a measured norm.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on b-roll

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on B-roll that pitches itself (Josh Blatchford) and Director Chair field notes on b-roll

items.name: Shoot the performance, generate the rest
items.effect: Real acting and timing, with the person, room or costume replaced by the model.
items.use_when: Ads where the budget goes to a performer, not to a set.
items.phrase: film the performance in a cheap plain room, then replace the person, the costume or the setting with Seedance 2.5 video edit, keeping the mouth and the timing

pitfalls.text: When the face and lipsync must stay exactly real, no generative edit works: they re-render the person. Use a matte and composite instead.
pitfalls.source: House rule

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on Seedance 2.5 character replacement

items.name: Animated ad from code, four steps
items.effect: A product ad in motion graphics without a timeline.
items.use_when: App and product ads of 8 to 20 seconds built by a coding model.
items.phrase: ingredients in one folder, a numbered storyboard approved before anything is animated, the build, then sound last

pitfalls.text: Give it the real logo and real screenshots. Without them a coding model draws a fake app and rebuilds the logo from shapes.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Per shot the storyboard states the voice line, what moves and how the shot becomes the next one. Approve it before the build.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Hold the real product next to the render: the model cannot see it, and the creator's first render had the wrong details.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Thirty minutes for two dollars is the creator's own figure for one ad; what it covers is not said, and his examples are spec ads, not client jobs.

items.name: Connector launch film
items.effect: The viewer sees that setting it up costs one line, then sees real answers.
items.use_when: Launching an MCP server, a connector or any integration.
items.phrase: eight beats in about 40 seconds: a competitor's number ticking up, the pain, the turn, the install in the host's own dialog, the question typed, the answer, one result card per data source, the payoff

pitfalls.text: Every result card carries the tool call that produced it, and the headline swaps words for live tokens; both make the answers read as real output.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Launch video structure on Poolday (Raphael Guilhem)

pitfalls.text: Build the host's dialog and chat from real screenshots, never an invented interface.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on motion graphics

pitfalls.text: The film it was measured from was posted behind a comment gate for a paid tool; the structure is visible in the film itself.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Launch video structure on Poolday (Raphael Guilhem)

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on motion graphics and Director Chair notes on Launch video structure on Poolday (Raphael Guilhem)

items.body:
## The beats, measured off a 40-second film

| Beat | Until | On screen |
|---|---|---|
| Hook | 4.8 s | a competitor's number ticking up |
| Pain | 10.1 s | the manual way: searching, tabs piling up |
| Turn | 13.1 s | the question that changes it, and the connector's name as a chip |
| Plug it in | 15.4 s | the host's own add-connector dialog, the address typed |
| Just ask | 18.4 s | the question typed into the chat |
| The answer | 25.7 s | the first result cards |
| Every channel | 37.1 s | one result card per data source |
| Payoff | 40 s | connected, then the logo |

items.name: Edit a take in the style of a reel you like
items.effect: The edit starts from a look that already works, not from settings.
items.use_when: Talking-head takes edited by an agent.
items.phrase: send the reel whose edit you like, ask for your own take to be cut in that style, review the result, then save the process for next time

pitfalls.text: The tools are free; the taste is in the reference. Neither creator who shows the method gives a measured result beyond his own views.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on One prompt edit (Payton Kaleiwahea, Mino)

pitfalls.text: An analysis done in one chat is lost when the chat ends. Capture the reference once: layout, caption style and timing, cut rhythm, inserts and effects, sound.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on One prompt edit (Payton Kaleiwahea, Mino)

pitfalls.text: The cost figures, about 1.14 dollars for a whole edit, are one creator's own count on his plan.

items.name: Feature drop
items.effect: One problem, one answer, and the real screen as the proof, in under half a minute.
items.use_when: Announcing one feature of a software product, 15 to 25 seconds.
items.phrase: hook, the problem, the reveal of the name, the product on screen, proof numbers ticking up, three features, the call to action

pitfalls.text: Beat lengths timed off two launch clips of 12 to 15 seconds: hook 2.5 seconds, problem 3, reveal 2.5, product 4, numbers 3, features 3, call to action 3.

items.effect: A long list goes by fast and still feels like one film.
items.use_when: N tools, N workflows, N of anything, with the full list in the post text.
items.phrase: one fixed mask holds the frame for the whole list, a horizon-shaped arc; each item is a new full-bleed texture inside it, cut hard on the beat, with a numbered two-line label at the bottom left

items.name: UGC at one table, seven setups
items.effect: A 15 to 25 second talking video that feels operated and alive, shot around one table.
items.use_when: Creator-style product ads with one person and one product.
items.phrase: seven lines, seven camera positions around one table, the camera at prop height, something near the lens in every shot, movement spent on the hook, calm by the end

pitfalls.text: For a restyle, shoot an empty room on purpose: plain walls, one table, one prop of the right shape; every object the model can map becomes part of the new world.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on UGC camera work (Higgsfield restyle demo, Abhinav Kalyan)

source.note: Our filming card in Director Chair notes on UGC camera work (Higgsfield restyle demo, Abhinav Kalyan)

items.body:
## The seven setups

| # | Camera | The person | Line |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | on the table at the near end, low and wide, pushing forward | stands at the far end with the product | the hook |
| 2 | at the table end beside a board, at tabletop height, sliding out from behind it | leans in on the elbows, product near the lens | the problem |
| 3 | across the table, starting tilted and ending level | leans on the forearms, product in both hands | the promise |
| 4 | high, looking down from the table end | stands beside the table, looks up | step one |
| 5 | flat on the tabletop | leans in and counts on the fingers | step two |
| 6 | in the hand at arm's length, slightly below the face | talks and reaches toward the lens | the social proof |
| 7 | on a tripod at chest height, three-quarter | ignores the camera and uses the product | the ask |

items.name: Read two numbers, then decide
items.effect: You know whether to fix the opening, fix the body, repeat or drop.
items.use_when: A post that has settled, about 72 hours after it went out.
items.phrase: compare reach and engagement with the account's own medians, never with another account

pitfalls.text: Reach without engagement: a fake-news opener had 490,000 plays at 1.0 percent likes and 0.18 percent saves, and led nowhere.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

pitfalls.text: Engagement without reach: the three weakest posts reached 7,600 to 11,700 views yet were saved at 0.9 to 3.4 percent, as much as the hits.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on short-form video (one TikTok account, 233 posts and 27 measured clips, read 30 Oct 2026)

items.body:
## The four outcomes

| | Engagement at or above the median | Engagement under half the median |
|---|---|---|
| **Reach 3 times or more** | A winner. Post the next one on the same promise within 48 hours | The opening works, the body or payoff does not. Keep frame 0, fix what follows |
| **Reach under half** | The body works, the opening did not stop people. New frame 0, re-cut, post again | Drop the idea |

Reach is views divided by the median of the account's ten posts before it. Engagement is likes, saves and shares per view against the account's own medians.

items.body:
## The usual pairs

| Sound | Event |
|---|---|
| Whoosh | a zoom, text sliding in |
| Riser | tension before a reveal |
| Click and impact | text or an object appearing |
| Ding | a right answer, good news |
| Cash register | money, a price |
| Camera shutter | a scene change, before and after |
| Shock | a pattern interrupt |
| Buzzer | a mistake, a myth debunked |

From a creator's TikTok series, collected in our hook framework. Pairs to start from, not rules.

items.name: Shallow depth of field
items.effect: Isolates the subject from a soft background; attention goes exactly where you want.
items.use_when: Portraits, product hero shots, interviews.
items.phrase: shallow depth of field, her eyes sharp, the café behind her a soft blur of shapes and lights

pitfalls.text: For stills, practitioners write a full capture line with an aperture (35mm, f/1.8); a 2025 study for Midjourney found f-stops ignored and plain words (blurred background) working. Plain words first, the number as support.
pitfalls.source: Dan Kieft (1 Sep 2026) via Director Chair field notes on image prompting; Midjourney mapping in our own notes (2025, to audit)

per_model.phrase: Employ a wide aperture of f/1.8 to create a shallow depth of field, rendering the background in soft, creamy bokeh while keeping the subject razor-sharp.

source.note: The first Director Chair spec, own words

items.name: Shape morph (every shot becomes the next)
items.effect: The eye always has one thing to follow, so a fast animated ad never loses the viewer at a cut.
items.use_when: Code-rendered product and app ads.
items.phrase: the price tag folds into a circle, the circle becomes the app icon, the icon opens into the home screen; each shot turns into the next, no dissolve

pitfalls.text: Left alone, a coding model builds separate shots and joins them with a cross-dissolve. Ask per pair of shots how this shape turns into that shape, and write the answer in the storyboard before anything is built.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: Fill the growing shape with the next shot's background colour first, then ease the next shot in from 93 to 100 percent; give the source object a squash of about 8 percent one pose before it grows.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath) (the style rules of his free skill, read 13 Nov 2026)

pitfalls.text: Review stills at three or four points inside every transition as well as at the holds.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

items.use_when: Any scene that holds longer than a second, animated or filmed.
items.phrase: a slow continuous push from 1.0 to 1.06 over the whole scene

pitfalls.text: Keep it subtle: a scale creep of 1 to 2 percent, or a push to about 1.06. This is the never-static move, not a zoom.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on motion graphics

pitfalls.text: One creator's rule for coded ads is that something always moves, even if it is only the camera, slowly.

items.name: Slow motion
items.effect: Stretches a moment so the viewer sees what the eye misses: water, hair, fabric, impact.
items.use_when: Product splashes, a decisive moment, sport, beauty.
items.phrase: slow motion, the splash rendered at high frame rate and played back slowly, every droplet visible

pitfalls.text: Ration it. Name the one or two moments in slow motion and keep the rest at normal speed, or it loses its weight.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting (Runway enhancer, tested prompts)

source.note: The first Director Chair spec and Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.name: Slow zoom in
items.effect: Builds tension or focus without the camera moving; the background flattens.
items.use_when: A realisation, a dramatic line, a product that should feel more and more important.
items.phrase: slow zoom in on her face, the camera stays in place while the lens tightens the frame

pitfalls.text: A zoom changes the lens and flattens the picture; a dolly moves the camera and keeps the depth. Say which one you mean.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.use_when: Ending a video, showing a person is not alone, revealing the setting.

pitfalls.text: A zoom keeps the perspective of one spot. For a reveal with depth, a dolly out reads more natural.

items.name: Smug
items.effect: Quiet superiority; the person knows they won.
items.use_when: Comparison ads, a winner, comedic confidence.
items.phrase: she half-closes her eyes, lets a slow lopsided smirk creep up on one side, raises her eyebrows once, tips her chin up a touch, and keeps looking straight at him with that smirk

pitfalls.text: Never ask for a smile or for an emotion by name; describe the muscles. Asked-for smiles come back generated and forced.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting (client feedback, Aug 2026)

pitfalls.text: Put the trigger first (the door slams, she reads the message), then the performance. Without a trigger the reaction has no timing.

licensed.name: Smug / Gloating
licensed.text: The eyelids lower, one corner of the mouth pulls into a slow smirk, the eyebrows rise once and settle, and the chin lifts slightly. The smirk holds through unbroken eye contact.

items.body:
## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** one mouth corner lifts, the lids lower slightly
- **Medium:** she half-closes her eyes, lets a slow lopsided smirk creep up on one side, raises her eyebrows once, tips her chin up a touch, and keeps looking straight at him with that smirk
- **Explosive:** leaning back with the hands behind the head, a wide knowing grin, a slow nod, the eyebrows raised

items.name: Snap or clap
items.effect: A gesture by the speaker triggers the change, so the cut feels caused.
items.use_when: Face cam into B-roll.
items.phrase: she snaps her fingers at the lens and on the snap the shot changes to the product on the table

pitfalls.text: Use one marker per kind of change and keep it for the whole video: a snap or clap from face to B-roll, a swipe between B-roll shots, a jump cut from face to face.
pitfalls.source: The Director Chair script structure notes

pitfalls.text: As an opening, the honest version is a gesture that becomes the product shot.

items.name: Sound hook
items.effect: Catches the viewer who has the sound on, in the same second as the picture.
items.use_when: The first second of every feed video.
items.phrase: one sound event in the first second: a whoosh on the push-in, or an impact as the text lands

pitfalls.text: One sound per visual event. Sound supports the voice and never competes with it.

items.effect: A claim arrives with its source on screen, so a story can stay fiction while its facts stay checkable.
items.use_when: Opinion pieces, future scenarios, awareness films.
items.phrase: the figure holds a printed page of the report toward the lens, its title readable

pitfalls.text: A stated fact with no source page on screen is the listed failure of the measured story reel.

items.effect: A muted viewer can tell who is talking.
items.use_when: Dialogue, interviews, any two-voice format.
items.phrase: a small name tag above each caption line, one colour per speaker, the spoken word in a highlighted pill

pitfalls.text: In the measured two-voice reference 243 of the visual changes sit in the caption band, against 49 in the call tiles and 46 in the shared screen. The captions carry the rhythm; the picture changes about once every 7 seconds.

items.name: Speaker over a board
items.effect: The face keeps the trust while the board shows the thing, and neither covers the other.
items.use_when: Tool tutorials, step lists, explainers with things to show.
items.phrase: split the vertical frame: the speaker in the top 29 percent as one continuous take, a board in a saturated brand colour in the lower 71 percent, captions on the seam

pitfalls.text: Measured shares: speaker 29 percent over a board of 71 in one reference, 39 over 61 in another. In both the speaker zone never cuts; all the pace comes from the board.

items.effect: The viewer wants to see how it ends before deciding to scroll.

items.phrase: the first frame is already mid-event: coffee leaving the cup toward the counter, a hand reaching to catch it

pitfalls.text: On a hook-teaching account, 18 of its 20 most viewed posts open on an event already under way in the first second; none of its three weakest does. One account in one niche: evidence, not a law.

## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** one eye narrows a fraction, the head stays still, the gaze holds
- **Medium:** the chin lowers while the eyes stay up, one brow rises higher than the other, the head turns slightly so the look comes from the side, one mouth corner tightens, the stare holds
- **Explosive:** a slow lean in, the eyes narrow to slits, the finger points, the head shakes slowly while the stare never breaks

items.name: Swipe
items.effect: The new shot pushes the old one out in the direction of the movement.

pitfalls.text: Use one marker per kind of change and keep it for the whole video: a snap or clap from face to B-roll, a swipe between B-roll shots, a jump cut from face to face.
pitfalls.source: The Director Chair script structure notes

pitfalls.text: In code-rendered video this is a push slide: the incoming scene pushes the old one out. It suits the scenes in the middle of a video.

items.name: Low push over the table

pitfalls.text: Measured on the reference: about 2.5 times closer in just over a second, eased out, then a hold. It is a physical move: the near edge of the table slides out under the lens.

pitfalls.text: Spend the movement on the hook. The camera calms down as the content gets denser.
