## Three intensities

- **Subtle:** the breath stops, the eyes fix on one point, the hands go still
- **Medium:** the brows lift and pull together, the eyes stay wide and unblinking, the mouth stretches open, the chin pulls back, the chest rises and falls fast and shallow
- **Explosive:** the body presses back against the wall, a scream with no sound, the hands claw at the surface behind, the eyes never leave the threat

items.name: One variable per test
items.effect: A result you can read: you know why the winner won.
items.use_when: Testing hooks and formats, organic or paid.
items.phrase: each variant gets an id, a hypothesis, the one thing it changes, what stays fixed, a cost, an observation window and the result that would justify the next test

pitfalls.text: Ten creatives that differ in everything can find a winner and still not tell you why.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on hooks and ideas

pitfalls.text: Stage A explores formats. Stage B tests three hooks on one body, character, demo and call to action.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on AI UGC army (Jake Castillo)

items.name: Six-stage voice chain
items.effect: A phone or clip-on recording sounds like a broadcast voice.
items.use_when: Every voice recorded outside a studio: creator video, a talking head, a podcast clip.
items.phrase: run the voice through a high-pass at 100 Hz, a downward expander, a de-esser, a 3 dB lift around 3.5 kHz, a compressor and a limiter, in that order

pitfalls.text: The expander goes before the compressor. Otherwise the compressor lifts the room noise between the words again.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Product UI as the explainer (Patchd)

pitfalls.text: Measured on the dry half of the source clip's own hook: the chain lowered the noise floor from -23.6 to -33.8 dB and kept the peaks under -1 dBFS. The values are starting points, not tuned to a room.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Product UI as the explainer (Patchd)

pitfalls.text: Set the expander's threshold above the room's own noise, measured on a second of silence. Loudness is a separate last step.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on editing

source.note: Own words from Director Chair notes on Product UI as the explainer (Patchd) and Director Chair field notes on editing

items.body:
## The six stages, in order

| # | Stage | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | High-pass at about 100 Hz | removes rumble, where there is almost no voice |
| 2 | Downward expander | turns the quiet moments down further, so fans, keys and breaths drop between words |
| 3 | De-esser | turns down only the sharp hiss of S sounds |
| 4 | Lift of 3 dB around 3,500 Hz | the range where words get their clarity |
| 5 | Compressor | narrows the gap between quiet and loud words |
| 6 | Limiter | a ceiling, so a laugh or a shout does not distort |

items.name: Voice first, then the face
items.effect: The mouth is generated for the voice that ships, not for one that is replaced later.
items.use_when: Generated people who speak: testimonials, ads, characters.
items.phrase: generate the final voice line first, with its delivery, then give that audio to the video model as the audio reference for the face

pitfalls.text: Not yet run by us. The order comes from a vendor launch whose film is a showreel of chosen takes; no failure rate is given.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Chimera (ElevenLabs, Eleven v4 with Seedance 2.5)

pitfalls.text: A voice reference used directly in the video model is often inconsistent between takes; the vendor's post and our own skill agree on that.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Chimera (ElevenLabs, Eleven v4 with Seedance 2.5)

pitfalls.text: A cloned voice speaking another language than its source loses its accent by design. Test before relying on an accent.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Chimera (ElevenLabs, Eleven v4 with Seedance 2.5) (the vendor's own documentation, read 22 Oct 2026)

pitfalls.text: Use your own voice or one with written consent.

items.name: Voice line
items.effect: The same voice in every generation of the film.
items.use_when: Dialogue across several generations.
items.phrase: voice: from Ghent, dry and clipped when frustrated, quiet and level when serious; with a voice recording bound as the reference

pitfalls.text: A voice recording as a reference keeps the voice stable across generations; text alone drifts.
pitfalls.source: Rourke Heath (25 Sep 2026) via Director Chair field notes on video prompting

source.note: Own words from Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.name: Voice-over written to the cut
items.effect: The voice ends when the picture does.
items.use_when: Ads with a fixed slot of 15 or 30 seconds.
items.phrase: write the voice-over to fit this 15-second animation, one line per shot, about 2.2 words per second, the last two seconds left free for the end card

pitfalls.text: A line typed into a voice tool without the timings is a guess: one creator shows a six-second voice-over delivered for a thirty-second slot.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

pitfalls.text: This order suits a fixed length. When the words lead, record the voice first and time the scenes to it.

items.name: Volumetric light
items.effect: Visible beams through haze: sacred, epic, atmospheric.
items.use_when: Churches, forests, warehouses, product reveals in haze.
items.phrase: light beams through the high windows, visible in the dust in the air, falling across the floor

pitfalls.text: Name what makes the beams visible (dust, haze, steam). Without it the model draws glowing stripes.
pitfalls.source: Not measured yet

per_model.phrase: Enhance the atmosphere with volumetric lighting, rendering visible rays of light cutting through haze or dust motes in the air.

items.name: What moves and what stays
items.effect: An animated photo that moves only where it should and does not look AI.
items.use_when: Animating a real photograph or an approved still.
items.phrase: real footage from a camera on a tripod, the frame identical at the start and the end; the water flows and the branches sway; the facade, the windows and the sign stay still

pitfalls.text: Motivate the locked frame instead of banning movement, name what moves small and physical, then list what stays still element by element, and name the sky colour or it washes out.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

pitfalls.text: An element that keeps failing: take it out of the image and give an end frame instead of tuning the prompt again.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.name: Which model for stills
items.effect: Picks the image model by the job instead of by the hype of the week.
items.use_when: Before writing any image prompt.
items.phrase: Nano Banana Pro by default; Nano Banana 2 for cheap test rounds; GPT Image 2.5 when the image carries text or a layout

pitfalls.text: A tutorial's model advice is an argument, not a rule: tutorials three weeks apart named different best models for skin. Compare with one image before switching.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

source.note: Own summary of Director Chair field notes on image prompting

items.body:
## The choice (checked 29 Sep 2026)

| Job | Model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Any still, by default | Nano Banana Pro | references hold best |
| Test rounds before the final | Nano Banana 2 | close to Pro for a fraction of the cost |
| Text, interface, typography on the image | GPT Image 2.5 | positioned for design and text |
| Character sheets, a second opinion | Seedream 5 | one tutorial's pick, not measured by us |

items.name: Which model for video
items.effect: Picks the video model by what the shot has to do.
items.use_when: Before writing any video prompt.
items.phrase: Seedance 2.5 for scenes with dialogue and characters; Kling 3.0 for short cheap single shots; Veo 3.1 for the most realistic motion from one still

pitfalls.text: A tutorial's model advice is an argument, not a rule: tutorials three weeks apart named different best models for skin. Compare with one image before switching.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

pitfalls.text: Kling 4.0 was announced on 27 Sep 2026 and was in closed beta; check availability before promising it.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on video prompting

source.note: Own summary of Director Chair field notes on video prompting

items.body:
## The choice (checked 29 Sep 2026)

| The shot has to | Model |
|---|---|
| Hold characters and dialogue over 10 to 30 seconds, several shots | Seedance 2.5 |
| Keep a real performance and change the person, the room or the costume | Seedance 2.5 video edit |
| Put a real person in a new setting, 3 to 10 seconds | Kling 3.0 Omni Edit |
| Move between a start frame and an end frame, flat animation, cheap | Kling 3.0 |
| Several shots from one start frame, more motion, 4 to 15 seconds | Seedance 2.0 |
| Look as real as possible in motion, 8 seconds or less, with sound | Veo 3.1 |

items.name: Whip pan
items.effect: A burst of energy that jumps attention from one thing to the next.
items.use_when: Transitions between two scenes, comedy beats, fast social edits.
items.phrase: whip pan, the camera snaps sideways from the first subject to the second in under half a second, motion blur during the turn, both ends sharp

pitfalls.text: A whip pan also hides continuity errors between two shots, which makes it a useful transition.
pitfalls.source: A 2026 model-syntax study for a prompt builder, summarised in Director Chair field notes on video prompting, not measured by us

licensed.name: Whip pan right
licensed.text: whip pan right. Movement: rotate rapidly from the starting direction toward a new target on the right. Speed: fast snap with brief motion blur during the rotation. Framing: begin on one readable composition and land on a second readable target. End: settle into a sharp final frame.

licensed.name: Whip pan left
licensed.text: whip pan left. Movement: rotate rapidly from the starting direction toward a new target on the left. Speed: fast snap with brief motion blur during the rotation. Framing: begin on one readable composition and land on a second readable target. End: settle into a sharp final frame.

source.note: Move names and the seven groups from aicameramovements.com (names and structure only); behaviour and numbers in our own words from Director Chair field notes on video prompting and the first Director Chair spec

items.body:
## Move card

- **Camera:** snaps sideways from one subject to another
- **Pace:** a fraction of a second, blurred in the middle
- **Keep:** a readable picture before and after the snap
- **Ends:** a sharp second subject

items.name: Whip between two subjects
items.effect: The blur of a fast swing hides the join and carries the energy from one subject to the next.
items.use_when: Handheld cutaways from the face to the screen, loops, changes of place.
items.phrase: handheld whip from his face to the monitor, the frame smearing for a few frames, landing on the screen

pitfalls.text: In a selfie diary measured at 2.57 visual changes per 10 seconds, the whip from the face to the monitor and back is the one camera move in the edit; everything else stays unproduced.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, 22 Oct 2026

items.name: Wide lens (24mm)
items.effect: Shows a lot of the place with a little drama in the perspective.
items.use_when: Establishing shots, interiors, low wide angles, geography of a scene.
items.phrase: 24mm wide lens, the whole interior visible, the person a few metres away

pitfalls.text: Focal length only means something with a sensor size. For Seedance, write the field of view in degrees plus the distance.
pitfalls.source: Field-of-view table from Higgsfield's tested Seedance prompts, via Director Chair field notes on video prompting

pitfalls.text: Degrees mean different things per tool: Camera Control uses a vertical field of view (29 degrees is about 50mm), Higgsfield's tested prompts a diagonal one (29 degrees is about 85mm). Say which, or give the focal length.
pitfalls.source: Camera Control (aicameracontrol.com), its framing label read on 13 Oct 2026 by placing the subject in the 3D stage and Director Chair field notes on video prompting

per_model.phrase: 84 degree diagonal field of view, camera 3 to 5 metres from the subject, no lens drift

items.name: Word drop
items.effect: One word lands with weight, and that is the word the viewer keeps.
items.use_when: The single claim or number in a talking-head line.
items.phrase: the key word falls in from above the frame and lands beside her head on the moment she says it

pitfalls.text: The effect fires on the word that names it. In the measured list reel an effect more than 0.2 seconds off its word is a listed failure.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair measurement of a published short, Oct 2026

pitfalls.text: One sound per visual event, under the voice.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Reel Kit (Justyn The AI Guy) (the kit's own craft rules)

items.name: Words slide up, one after another
items.effect: Text arrives in reading order and feels designed.
items.use_when: Headlines in animated ads and launch films.
items.phrase: each word rises into place from just below its line and sharpens from a slight blur, three to four frames after the word before

pitfalls.text: Our values: opacity 0 to 1, a rise of about 0.45 em, blur 10 pixels to 0, eased out, 3 to 4 frames between words. Let one key word dominate in size and accent colour.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on motion graphics

pitfalls.text: One creator's rule for coded ads: no bounce and no per-letter fades.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair notes on Motion graphics with Claude (Rourke Heath)

items.name: Worm's-eye view
items.effect: Exaggerates height and power: the ground sits at the lens and the subject towers above it.
items.use_when: Sneakers, tall buildings, a jump, a dramatic product reveal.
items.phrase: worm's-eye view, the lens on the ground looking straight up, the shoes in the foreground and the person towering above

pitfalls.text: Angles given in degrees and margins given as numbers are often ignored. Describe where the lens is against the body (at knee height, above her head) instead.
pitfalls.source: Director Chair field notes on image prompting

items.effect: A one-second mystery: what am I looking at?
items.use_when: Product details, before and after, a workspace.
items.phrase: start on a macro of the weave of the fabric, then pull back in one move to show the whole jacket on its hanger

pitfalls.text: Done in the edit it is a digital zoom, which needs 4K footage.

items.name: Zoom through
items.effect: The viewer flies into the product, and the next scene starts from inside it.
items.use_when: From an overview into one feature; the punchiest change in a montage.
items.phrase: the dashboard card scales up past the edges of the frame, blurred at the midpoint, and the next scene grows from small behind it

pitfalls.text: Put motion blur on the one or two fastest frames only; blur on every frame multiplies the render time.
